abstract: Software development sessions often involve several unfinished tasks rather than one issue carried through to completion. As coding agents take on repository-level development, they need to recover an earlier task’s requirements and partial progress after intervening work. Existing repository-level benchmarks typically score one issue-to-patch episode and do not directly measure whether an agent can resume a task after advancing other unfinished work in the same repository. We introduce Switch-SWE, a benchmark for focus-task resumption in sessions that interleave unfinished tasks drawn from the same source repository, with a persistent checkout for each task. Each focus task is evaluated in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical focus requirements and executable verifiers. The switched session interleaves ordered stages from other unfinished tasks in the same repository, while only the final focus patch is scored. Switch-SWE contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, reconstructed from issue, pull-request, and review histories and rendered as 400 matched session specifications. Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average focus-task resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0 percentage points. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent resumption behaviors. We introduce a plug-in context-management module that selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries. On OpenCode, the module improves focus-task completion under same-repository task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models. Code is available at github.com/Miraclecsc/Switch-SWE.

sections.body: The section motivates Switch-SWE, a benchmark that tests whether a coding agent can resume an unfinished repository task after advancing other unfinished tasks from the same repository in one session. Each focus task is run in a matched uninterrupted session and a switched session with identical requirements and verifier. Across 7 agents, interleaved work produces an average resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent failures. The section also introduces a plug-in context-management module that improves focus-task completion on OpenCode by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Coding agents must resume unfinished tasks after intervening work, and existing benchmarks do not directly measure this.

sections.body: The section places Switch-SWE among four related areas. Repository-level benchmarks such as SWE-bench score single issue-to-patch episodes. Long-horizon benchmarks such as SWE-Marathon and ChainSWE study sustained or cumulative work. Task-recovery and interactive work, including ContinuityBench and SWE-Touch, studies recovery from preserved states, handoffs, or user edits. Context-management methods maintain memories over long sessions. The authors state that Switch-SWE differs by keeping one agent in a continuous session where the intervening work consists of other unfinished tasks in the same repository.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work covers repository benchmarks, long-horizon development, task recovery, and context management, but not same-repository task switching.

sections.body: Each task is a repository snapshot, an ordered list of substantive requests, and an executable verifier. Requests come from issue, pull-request, and review histories. The switched schedule preserves the focus task's request order and verifier, and interleaves ordered stages from four other tasks in the same repository. Each task keeps a persistent checkout, and interruptions are selected as near or far by whether they share an immediate source directory with the focus task. Only the final focus patch is scored, using held-out tests. The benchmark contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, giving 400 session specifications.
sections.heading: Switch-SWE
sections.headline: Switch-SWE pairs each focus task with an uninterrupted control and a switched session that interleaves four other unfinished same-repository tasks.

sections.body: Resolution is measured on final focus patches in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions. The average gap is 11.5 percentage points, from 6.0 for GLM-5.3 with OpenCode to 15.0 for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with OpenCode. All seven configurations show larger gaps for far interruptions than near ones, with averages of 14.9 and 8.1. Switched sessions use 4.5 to 11.1 times as many tokens as uninterrupted sessions. The authors note that the locality association does not establish a causal effect. Each agent invocation has a 900-second budget, with at most three timeout continuations per session, and at most two retries for confirmed infrastructure faults.
sections.heading: Experimental Results
sections.headline: Across seven configurations, switching lowers focus-task resolution by an average of 11.5 points, and far interruptions cause larger gaps than near ones.

sections.body: The Resumption Context Manager has two parts: a Task History Router that selects interaction groups for the active and related tasks, and Task State Memory that records goal, constraints, progress, and pending work for each task. For models on OpenCode, the +Router variant raises switched resolution by 11.0 points for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and 3.5 points for GLM-5.3, with uninterrupted resolution changing by -1.0 and +0.5 points. Adding memory improves switched resolution by a further 4.5 points for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and 2.0 points for GLM-5.3. The full RCM leaves uninterrupted resolution within 0.5 points of native OpenCode. The authors note that these results do not establish a benefit from switching itself.
sections.heading: Context Management for Task Resumption
sections.headline: A plug-in context manager routes task-relevant history and keeps task-state memory, and it narrows the switched-task gap on OpenCode.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the benchmark: 200 focus tasks from 19 repositories, with matched uninterrupted and switched sessions. Seven configurations show an average resolution gap of 11.5 percent under switching within one repository. The authors conclude that code persistence alone does not ensure reliable resumption. The Resumption Context Manager improves switched resolution by 5.5 to 15.5 percent on OpenCode while maintaining comparable uninterrupted performance.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Switched sessions lower resolution on average, and the proposed context manager raises switched completion on OpenCode.

sections.body: The statement says generative AI models served as the evaluated coding agents and as auxiliary components of the proposed Resumption Context Manager. The authors also report using generative AI tools for interpreting results, debugging research code, summarizing literature, revising text, and developing plotting scripts. They state that AI tools did not generate synthetic benchmark data, clean or reformat benchmark data, or perform qualitative classification of trajectories. The authors state that they reviewed all AI-assisted work and remain responsible for the final content.
sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.headline: The authors disclose their use of generative AI as coding agents, as auxiliary model components, and for writing, debugging, and figure work.

sections.body: The ethics statement says the benchmark is built from repository repair tasks and development histories drawn from public software projects. It states that the purpose is to characterize how reliably agents resume unfinished work. The authors state that the work is not meant to assess the performance of individual developers or repository contributors.
sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.headline: The work uses repair tasks and development histories from public projects and aims to characterize agent reliability, not individual developers.

sections.body: The reproducibility statement lists where the benchmark and evaluation are documented. Section 3 covers task construction, matched schedules, source-directory locality, and executable verification. Appendix C gives construction and schedule-validation details. Appendix B covers configurations, execution environments, the request interface, scoring, and resource accounting. Section 5.2 and Appendix F describe the Resumption Context Manager, and Section 5.3 presents its evaluation. The authors plan to publicly release the benchmark data and code.
sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.headline: The paper points to the sections and appendices that define construction, schedules, scoring, and the context manager, and promises a public release.

sections.body: Table 4 compares Switch-SWE with SWE-bench, SWE-bench-Live, SWE-ContextBench, InterruptBench, and SWE-Touch on size, repositories, and capabilities such as interleaved tasks and persistent per-task workspaces. Appendix B lists harnesses, models, versions, the runtime environment, the request interface, and the scoring and accounting protocol. Appendix C covers construction, test classification, and interruption selection. Appendix E gives trajectory examples of requirement-state loss and of focus-identity confusion during submission. Appendix F describes the Router and Task State Memory implementation on OpenCode.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix compares Switch-SWE with related benchmarks and gives harness, scoring, and context-manager implementation details with worked trajectory examples.
